title: Relative clauses
tagline: Add extra information about people, things, places and time — all in one longer, smarter sentence.
why: Relative clauses let you give extra information about a noun without starting a new sentence, and B1 Preliminary tests them constantly: the open cloze often has a missing who, which or whose, and photo descriptions sound far more natural with 'a boy who is wearing a red cap' than with two short sentences. Get the pronoun and the comma right and both your writing and your speaking sound like a real B1 candidate.

hook.text: Sofia points at a house. "That's the family who just moved in." Nadia: "The ones whose dog barks all night?" Sofia: "That's them — the house where the old bakery used to be."
hook.ask: Sofia uses who, whose and where to add information about the family, the dog and the house. Which word points to a person, which one shows something belongs to someone, and which one points to a place?

diagrams.title: Join two sentences into one

before.text: I know a family. The family just moved in.

after.text: I know a family who just moved in.

steps: Find the noun that both sentences share.
Delete it from the second sentence.
Put who (people), which (things) or where (places) in its place.
Join the two sentences into one, with no full stop in the middle.
diagrams.caption: One relative pronoun does the job of a whole repeated noun.

rows.label: What it does
cells: Says exactly which person or thing you mean

rows.label: Commas?
cells: Yes — one comma before, one after (or at the end)

rows.label: Remove it?
cells: No — the sentence loses its meaning
Yes — the sentence still makes sense without it

rows.label: Can you use that?
cells: No — never that straight after a comma

rows.label: Example
cells: The boy who sits next to me is Peruvian.
Mateo, who sits next to me, is Peruvian.

diagrams.title: Build a relative clause

sentences.note: who = subject of its own clause (who lives…)
that is optional — it's the object of reading
whose shows the dog belongs to the boy

diagrams.caption: The clause starts right after the noun it describes — as close as possible.

formula.chip: who / which / that / whose / where / when

head: Pronoun
Refers to
Example
rows: a person, as subject or object
a thing, as subject or object
a person or thing (informal, defining only)

use.point: Who, which and that: naming exactly who or what you mean

examples.text: The girl who sits next to Mateo is new.
examples.note: who = person, subject of the clause

examples.text: I didn't like the film that we watched last night.
examples.note: that = thing, informal and very common

examples.text: Miss Vega is the teacher who also coaches the football team.
examples.note: adds essential information about which teacher

examples.text: Nadia found the keys which I lost yesterday.
examples.note: which = thing, a little more formal than that

use.point: Whose, where and when: possession, place and time

examples.text: That's the boy whose sister is in our class.
This is the park where we play football on Sundays.
examples.note: where = place, instead of in which

examples.text: Sunday is the day when the market opens early.
examples.note: when = time, instead of on which

use.point: Leaving out the pronoun when it is the object

examples.text: The pizza (that) we ordered was cold.
examples.note: that is optional — it's the object of ordered

examples.text: Have you met the boy (who) Sofia is talking to?
examples.note: the pronoun can disappear when it isn't the subject

examples.text: The photos (which) Liam took are great.
examples.note: you can drop which/that here, but never a pronoun that is the subject

use.point: Non-defining clauses: extra information, not essential

examples.text: Mateo, who is Nadia's cousin, lives on our street.
examples.note: commas around extra info — the sentence works without it

examples.text: Cusco, where my grandmother was born, is in the mountains.
examples.note: a comma before and a comma after the clause

examples.text: My phone, which I bought last year, stopped working.
examples.note: which, never that, is used right after a comma

watch_out.wrong: The people which live next door are noisy.
watch_out.right: The people who live next door are noisy.
watch_out.why: which is for things; use who for people.

watch_out.wrong: Mateo, that is my cousin, is 14.
watch_out.why: Never use that straight after a comma — only who or which.

watch_out.wrong: The boy who his dog is brown lives here.
watch_out.right: The boy whose dog is brown lives here.
watch_out.why: Use whose for possession, not who + his/her together.

watch_out.wrong: The film that I saw it was boring.
watch_out.right: The film that I saw was boring.
watch_out.why: Don't repeat the object pronoun (it) — that already does that job.

watch_out.wrong: This is the restaurant which we ate dinner.
watch_out.right: This is the restaurant where we ate dinner.
watch_out.why: A clause about a place usually needs where, not which, with no preposition left over.

watch_out.wrong: The teacher who teach us Science is new.
watch_out.right: The teacher who teaches us Science is new.
watch_out.why: The verb still agrees with the noun before who (teacher = he/she).

l1.es: La gente que vive aquí es simpática.
l1.why: people is a plural noun in English, even though gente feels singular in Spanish.

l1.es: El chico cuyo perro ladra mucho.
l1.wrong: The boy who his dog barks a lot.
l1.right: The boy whose dog barks a lot.
l1.why: Spanish cuyo becomes whose — don't add his/her as well.

l1.wrong: The book that I bought it.
l1.why: In Spanish que never disappears, but the English pronoun it is not repeated — that already does the job.

l1.wrong: The day where I was born.
l1.why: que after a time word becomes when in English — where is only for places.

remember.trick: People who, things which, places where, owners whose!
remember.tip: If you can remove the clause and the sentence still makes sense, no commas are needed — that's a defining clause.

dialogue.title: The new neighbour
dialogue.context: Sofia and Nadia see removal vans outside a house on their street and talk about the family moving in, while Mateo tries to guess who they are.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Look — that's the family who just moved into the blue house.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: The ones whose dog barks every morning?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Exactly. The house is the one where the old bakery used to be.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Do you know the boy who was carrying all those boxes?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That's their son. He's the one whose bike is parked outside.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Is he the boy (who) you saw at the park last week?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Maybe! I only remember the day when he nearly fell off it.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: The bike (that) he rides is really cool, actually.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Let's say hello tomorrow, the day when school starts again.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Good idea. I hope he's someone who likes football.

items.why: who = person, subject of the clause

items.sentence: This is the café ___ we always meet.
Mateo, ___ is Nadia's cousin, lives near school.
items.why: who after a comma, never that

This is the town. I was born in this town.

can_do: I can add information about a person, thing or place using who, which, that or where.
I can use whose to show that something belongs to someone, and when for a time.
I can leave out who/which/that when it isn't the subject, and use commas for extra information.
summary: Relative clauses join two sentences into one by adding information about a noun.
Who and that are for people; which and that are for things; whose = possession; where = place; when = time.
Defining clauses (no commas) say exactly who or what you mean; non-defining clauses (with commas) add extra facts.
You can drop who/which/that when it is the object of the clause, but never when it is the subject.
That never follows a comma — only who or which introduce non-defining clauses.
